name: Ancient Greece
description: The foundational civilization of Western philosophy, mathematics, democracy, dramatic arts, and the Olympic games.

kingdoms.title: Argead Dynasty & Macedonian Empire
kingdoms.description: Northern Greek kingdom transformed by Philip II and Alexander the Great, which conquered the Persian Empire and spread Hellenistic culture to the Indus River.

kingdoms.title: Classical Athens & Delian League
kingdoms.description: The cradle of Western democracy, philosophy, theatre, and classical art, flourishing during the Golden Age of Pericles and the construction of the Acropolis.

sections.heading: Foundations of Democracy & Thought
content: Victories at Marathon and Salamis against Persian invaders
Golden Age of Pericles and construction of the Parthenon
Philosophical breakthroughs by Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle

kingdoms.title: Kingdom of Sparta (Lacedaemon)
kingdoms.description: Doric Greek military powerhouse renowned for its dual kingship, Agoge martial system, and pivotal role in the Greco-Persian and Peloponnesian Wars.

kings.title: Alexander III the Great (Basileus of Macedon)
kings.biography: Undefeated conqueror who overthrew the Persian Empire, founded over twenty cities bearing his name (including Alexandria), and forged an empire from Greece to Egypt and the Indus River by age 32.
kings.internationalConnections: Fused Greek, Persian, Egyptian, and Central Asian cultures, sparking the global Hellenistic Era.

kings.title: King Leonidas I of Sparta
kings.biography: Agiad King of Sparta whose heroic stand with 300 Spartan warriors and Greek allies at the Battle of Thermopylae against Xerxes' massive Persian invasion became an eternal symbol of courage.
kings.internationalConnections: Commanded the unified Greek land forces defending against the Achaemenid Persian invasion.

kings.title: King Philip II of Macedon
kings.biography: Visionary military reformer who created the devastating Macedonian sarissa phalanx, unified Greece under the League of Corinth, and laid the foundations for his son Alexander's world conquests.
kings.internationalConnections: United the Greek city-states for a planned pan-Hellenic expedition against the Persian Empire.

kings.title: Pericles (Strategos of Athens)
kings.biography: The foremost statesman, general, and orator of classical Athens who promoted radical democracy, fostered arts and philosophy, and commissioned the construction of the Parthenon on the Acropolis.
kings.internationalConnections: Led the Delian League against Persian influence in Egypt and Cyprus, transforming Athens into the naval hegemon of the Aegean.

sites.name: Colossus of Rhodes
sites.description: Gigantic 33-meter bronze titan dedicated to the sun god Helios, an Ancient World Wonder.
sites.history: Erected to commemorate the successful defense of Rhodes against a year-long siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305 BCE. Financed by selling the abandoned siege engines and weaponry left behind by the besiegers.
sites.construction: Crafted from melted siege bronze and iron over stone-weighted interior masonry towers, standing approximately 33 meters (108 feet) high at the harbor entrance.
sites.architecture: Portrayed the sun god Helios with a radiant crown, holding a torch or spear overlooking Mandraki harbor.
sites.significance: The tallest and most ambitious bronze statue in antiquity, inspiring future monuments including the Statue of Liberty.
sites.currentStatus: Destroyed by the 226 BCE Rhodes earthquake after standing for only 54 years; the fallen bronze ruins lay undisturbed for 800 years until sold for scrap in 653 CE.
sites.wonderReplacedBy: Replaced in modern global canon by the New 7 Wonders campaign
sites.wonderHistoricalContext: Though standing for only 54 years before the 226 BCE earthquake broke its knees, an oracle warned the Rhodians against rebuilding it. Even in ruin, Pliny the Elder wrote that 'few men can clasp its thumb, and its fingers are larger than most statues.' In 653 CE, Arab caliphate forces sold the bronze to a merchant from Edessa.

sites.name: Parthenon on the Acropolis
sites.description: The quintessential Doric marble temple of Athena, an official New 7 Wonders Top Global Finalist.
sites.history: Built during the Golden Age of Athens under Pericles as the centerpiece of the Acropolis complex, housing the giant chryselephantine statue of Athena Parthenos.
sites.construction: Constructed from 20,000 tons of white Pentelic marble with subtle optical entasis curves so the lines appear perfectly straight to the human eye.
sites.architecture: Peripteral octastyle Doric temple with Ionic frieze elements, pediment sculptures, and metopes depicting battles of gods, giants, and centaurs.
sites.significance: The enduring global symbol of Western democracy, classical philosophy, and architectural harmony. Official Top 21 Finalist in the 2007 New 7 Wonders campaign.
sites.currentStatus: Standing and conserved on the Acropolis rock in Athens.
sites.wonderCategory: New7Wonders Top Global Finalist & Ancient Masterpiece
sites.wonderHistoricalContext: Celebrated for 2,500 years as the highest peak of Greek classical architecture, finishing in the premier Top 21 Global Finalists in the official 2007 New 7 Wonders worldwide ballot.

sites.name: Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi
sites.description: The sacred center ('omphalos' or navel) of the ancient Greek world, home to the revered Pythian Oracle of Apollo.
sites.history: Leaders from every Greek city-state and foreign kings consulted the Pythia priestess before waging war or establishing colonies.
sites.construction: Perched on the slopes of Mount Parnassus, featuring Doric stone temples, treasury houses, an open-air theatre, and athletic stadium.
sites.architecture: Features the Temple of Apollo, Athenian Treasury, the circular Tholos of Delphi at the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia.
sites.significance: UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987; the spiritual heartbeat of pan-Hellenic unity.
sites.currentStatus: Preserved archaeological park in Phocis, Greece.

sites.name: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
sites.description: Colossal 12.4-meter chryselephantine statue of the king of Greek gods, an Ancient World Wonder.
sites.history: Commissioned by the Eleans for the sanctuary at Olympia, the statue was sculpted by Phidias. Zeus sat upon an elaborate cedarwood throne ornamented with ebony, ivory, gold, and precious gemstones, holding Nike (goddess of victory) in his right hand.
sites.construction: Framed with wood and paneled with sculpted ivory plates for flesh and beaten sheets of solid gold for drapery (chryselephantine technique).
sites.architecture: The statue occupied the entire width of the cella aisle in the Temple of Zeus, appearing so grand that ancient writers remarked if Zeus stood up, he would unroof the temple.
sites.significance: The crowning achievement of ancient Greek classical sculpture and an essential pilgrimage destination during the Ancient Olympic Games.
sites.currentStatus: Destroyed in the 5th century CE by fire (either at Olympia in 426 CE or during the Palace of Lausus fire in Constantinople in 475 CE).
sites.wonderReplacedBy: Replaced in modern global canon by the New 7 Wonders campaign
sites.wonderHistoricalContext: Admired across the Greco-Roman world for eight centuries. After the abolition of the Olympic Games by Christian Emperor Theodosius I, the statue was relocated to Constantinople, where it perished in a palace conflagration in 475 CE.

sites.name: Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
sites.builtBy: Croesus of Lydia / Chersiphron / Alexander the Great
sites.description: Colossal marble sanctuary with 127 ionic columns, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
sites.history: Dedicated to Artemis, goddess of fertility and the hunt, the temple was funded by the wealthy King Croesus of Lydia. Arsoned in 356 BCE by Herostratus on the night Alexander the Great was born, it was rebuilt on an even grander scale with Alexander's backing.
sites.construction: Built entirely of white marble spanning 137 meters in length and 69 meters in width, featuring 127 carved columns standing 18 meters high.
sites.architecture: Magnificent Ionic dipteral temple surrounded by a double row of columns adorned with bas-reliefs by renowned sculptors Scopas and Polyclitus.
sites.significance: The largest temple in the Hellenistic world, serving as a religious sanctuary, financial bank, and cultural trade nexus.
sites.currentStatus: Destroyed in 401 CE by a mob led by St. John Chrysostom; only a single reconstructed composite column remains at the site near Selçuk, Turkey.
sites.wonderReplacedBy: Replaced in modern global canon by the New 7 Wonders campaign
sites.wonderHistoricalContext: Antipater of Sidon wrote: 'When I saw the sacred house of Artemis that towers to the clouds, the other Wonders were placed in the shade.' It was pillaged by Goths in 268 CE and finally dismantled in 401 CE.
